v.q: What is the main goal of normalising a relational schema?
o: Remove redundancy so each fact is stored once and stays consistent
Make every query faster by joining fewer tables
Keep each table on a separate database server
Convert all columns to text so types never clash
v.w: Duplicated facts drift apart and cause update, insert and delete anomalies. Normalisation trades some join cost for correctness.

v.q: Which statement about normalisation is NOT true?
o: It always makes every query faster
It reduces duplicated data
It prevents update anomalies
It keeps each fact in one place
v.w: Normalisation protects consistency. It often needs more joins, so reads can get slower.

v.q: A table has a column `phones` holding "555-1234, 555-9876". Which normal form does this violate?
o: First normal form: values must be atomic
Second normal form: no partial dependencies
Third normal form: no transitive dependencies
Boyce-Codd normal form: every determinant is a key
v.w: 1NF requires one value per cell and no repeating groups. Move phones into a child table with one row per number.

v.q: Which design satisfies first normal form for storing a customer's phone numbers?
o: One row per phone number in a child table
A comma-separated text column
A column named phones
A JSON string in one column
v.w: First normal form needs atomic values, so each number is its own row.

v.q: In a table keyed by (`order_id`, `product_id`), the column `product_name` depends only on `product_id`. What is this?
o: A partial dependency, which breaks 2NF
A transitive dependency, which breaks 3NF
A multi-valued dependency, which breaks 4NF
An ordinary dependency that every table needs
v.w: A non-key column must depend on the whole composite key. Move product details into a `product` table.

v.q: In a table keyed by (order_id, product_id), which column shows a partial dependency?
o: product_name, which depends on product_id
quantity, which depends on both columns
The order_id key column
The product_id key column
v.w: A column that depends on only part of a composite key breaks second normal form.

v.q: A customer table stores `branch_id`, `branch_city` and `branch_manager`. `branch_city` is determined by `branch_id`. Which rule does that break?
o: Third normal form: non-key columns depend only on the key
First normal form: values must be atomic
Second normal form: no partial dependencies
Fourth normal form: no multi-valued dependencies
v.w: That is a transitive dependency: customer to branch to city. Split out a `branch` table.

v.q: A table stores zip_code and city, and city is determined by zip_code. Which dependency is this?
o: Transitive
Partial
Multi-valued
Atomic
v.w: A non-key column depends on another non-key column, so the key is not the only determinant. It breaks third normal form.

v.q: Which anomaly happens when you cannot record a new product until someone orders it?
o: Insertion anomaly
Update anomaly
Deletion anomaly
Rollback anomaly
v.w: Mixing facts about different entities in one table forces unrelated data to be stored together. Deleting the last order could also erase the product (deletion anomaly).

v.q: Which anomaly happens when deleting an order also loses the only record of a product?
o: Deletion anomaly
Insertion anomaly
Update anomaly
Phantom anomaly
v.w: Unrelated facts stored together are lost when one row goes. Separate tables avoid it.

v.q: Why do reporting or read-heavy systems sometimes denormalise on purpose?
o: It avoids costly joins on reads, at the price of duplicated data
Normalised tables cannot carry any indexes
Relational databases do not support joins at all
It reduces the storage taken by every row
v.w: Denormalisation is a deliberate trade: faster reads against extra write work and the risk of inconsistency. Do it after measuring.

v.q: Which statement about denormalisation is NOT true?
o: It removes the risk of inconsistent copies
It can speed up reads
It duplicates data on purpose
It must be kept in sync
v.w: Duplicated data can drift apart, so denormalisation adds a risk instead of removing it.

v.q: What does 3NF informally say about a non-key column?
o: It depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key
It may depend on any other non-key column
It must be unique across the whole table
It must always carry an index
v.w: A well-known mnemonic: the key (1NF), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF).

v.q: Which phrase summarises third normal form?
o: The key, the whole key and nothing but the key
Every column holds no null values
Every column has its own index
Every table lives in one database
v.w: Every non-key column must depend on the key directly, and on all of it.

v.q: A payments table keeps a copy of the customer's name for each row, so that old statements still show the old name. Is this a normalisation bug?
o: Not necessarily: it is a deliberate snapshot of history
Yes, it always breaks first normal form
Yes, it must instead be a foreign key to the current name
No, because names are never normalised
v.w: Records such as invoices and statements should preserve what was true at the time. A snapshot is a different fact from the current name.

v.q: Which table design for invoices is a deliberate denormalisation?
o: Storing the billed customer name on each invoice
Keeping two copies of the same price list
Repeating the product name in each order line without reason
A comma-separated list of invoice ids
v.w: The name at billing time is part of the document history and must not change when the customer renames.
